newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane Danny's path may keep U.S. Midwest dry.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Danny's path may keep U.S. Midwest dry.

text.p: Hurricane Danny's slow northeasterly course into the southeast United States should deprive most U.S. Midwest crop production areas of significant moisture this weekend, meteorologists said.
"We don't look for anything very heavy or very big coverage," said Peter Leavitt, CEO of Weather Services Corp, referring to Midwest rain generated by the hurricane.
Leavitt said Danny was expected to slowly move northeast into Alabama and Tennessee, which should keep rain south of the Ohio River Valley.

The storm's quick surge to hurricane status surprised meteorologists, causing some to change their forecasts. Weather Express Inc's Fred Gesser, who on Thursday expected the storm to push rain into the Midwest, said Friday the Hurricane's path will keep rain out of the Midwest.
"As a result it will not spread moisture up into Illinois and Missouri," he said.
The high pressure system over the Midwest should remain in place through the weekend, possibly being displaced Tuesday by a cold front now over the Dakotas, said Gesser.

Scattered showers of 0.10 to 0.50 inch were likely Friday through Sunday across northern Illinois, and amounts of 0.50 to two inches were forecast for southern Minnesota, northeast Iowa and the Dakotas, said Gesser.

A tropical storm developing near the Bahamas and moving west could push rain from the remnants of Danny back into the Midwest, Gesser said. But he said that was too far in the future to accurately forecast.
Freese-Notis Weather Inc also doubts Hurricane Danny will impact Midwest weather, but it does forecast chances of rain for the dry areas of central Illinois.

"There is plenty of low-level atmospheric moisture in the Midwest," said Craig Solberg, Freese-Notis meteorologist. "We still expect good rain in the driest areas of the Midwest the next couple of days."

Elsewhere, the Dakotas continued to receive abundant rain. About 0.50 to 1.5 inches fell since late Thursday over much of the area. Another 0.50 inch was likely this weekend with clear weather likely early next week, said Solberg.
"In areas where the (spring wheat) crop is headed, they probably would like to see some drying out," Solberg said.
Clear weekend weather was forecast for the Kansas and Nebraska hard red winter wheat areas.
"It looks like a good weekend for harvesting winter wheat," he said.
